content.title: About
content.content: Lentils are an annual legume cultivated for its edible seeds. Originating from the Mediterranean and Western Asia, they are now grown worldwide. Lentils have a mild, slightly earthy flavor, a firm yet tender texture, and come in several colors: green, brown, red, and black.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils belong to the Fabaceae family and are among the oldest cultivated crops – they were grown in ancient Egypt.
More than 50 lentil varieties exist, differing in color, size, and maturation time.
Red lentils cook the fastest – they are ready in 15‑20 minutes.
Lentils are protein‑rich, making them a popular meat substitute in vegetarian and vegan diets.
Global lentil production exceeded 5 million tonnes in the 2020s.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of cooked lentils provides about 9 g of protein, offering a valuable amino acid profile for plant‑based nutrition.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Lentils contain roughly 8 g of fiber per 100 g, supporting healthy digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The slow release of carbohydrates helps stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in iron and folate
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport, while folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lentils provide polyphenols and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to lentils, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of minerals such as iron and zinc. Soaking and sprouting lower its level.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Legumes, including lentils, can cause increased gas in sensitive individuals. Gradual introduction helps the digestive system adapt.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: People with gout are advised to limit lentil intake due to its moderate purine levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lentils can be boiled, stewed, added to soups, salads, stews, and veggie patties. They are also used to make purees, lentil flour for baking, and as a meat‑like filler in dishes. Soaking for 2‑4 hours speeds cooking and improves digestibility.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry lentils in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, they keep for 2‑3 years. Cooked lentils should be refrigerated and consumed within 4‑5 days.
